examples.name: An active filter
examples.description: The common case - a property name plus its current value, editable in place via the value segment's own menu.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Status"
  elemBefore={<TaskNotStartedIcon decorative />}
  value={{
    label: '2 statuses',
    sections: [
      {
        id: 'statuses',
        items: [
          { id: 'not-started', label: 'Not started', onSelect: () => toggleStatus('not-started') },
          { id: 'in-progress', label: 'In progress', onSelect: () => toggleStatus('in-progress') },
        ],
      },
    ],
  }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')}
/>

examples.name: A filter with a comparison operator
examples.description: An optional operator segment sits between the label and the value. Figma only shows this on its due date filter, but nothing about it is date-specific.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Due date"
  elemBefore={<CalendarIcon decorative />}
  operator={{
    label: 'before',
    sections: [{ id: 'ops', items: [{ id: 'on', label: 'on' }, { id: 'before', label: 'before' }, { id: 'after', label: 'after' }] }],
  }}
  value={{ label: 'April 15', sections: dateSections }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('due')}
/>

examples.name: A filter whose value has a preview
examples.description: valuePreview renders before the value text - an Avatar, an Avatar Group, status icons. Decorative only; the value text carries the meaning.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Assignee"
  value={{ label: '3 people', sections: peopleSections }}
  valuePreview={
    <AvatarGroup
      size="xs"
      maxVisible={3}
      avatars={[
        { id: 'a', name: 'Jordan Ellis' },
        { id: 'b', name: 'Priya Nair' },
        { id: 'c', name: 'Sam Okafor' },
      ]}
    />
  }
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('assignee')}
/>

examples.name: An applied property
examples.description: The value is the label, so there is nothing to open - the only affordance is removing it.

examples.name: A selectable search scope
examples.description: scope is the only selectable mode - a real toggle button carrying aria-pressed. Chip never changes its own selection; wire onSelectedChange.

examples.name: Smaller size for a dense filter bar
examples.description: size applies to every segment together, matching Figma - there is no per-segment size mixing.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  size="sm"
  label="Status"
  value={{ label: 'Any', sections: statusSections }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')}
/>

examples.name: Naming a panel explicitly
examples.description: Panels default to `${label} value` / `${label} operator`. Override when the composed name would read poorly, or when label is not a plain string.
examples.jsx: Status} value={{ label: '2 statuses', sections: statusSections, menuAriaLabel: 'Choose statuses' }} removeAriaLabel="Clear the status filter" onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')} />

antiExamples.name: Using Chip as a plain label
antiExamples.reason: Only if there is nothing to remove. A non-removable, non-interactive label is Tag's job - Chip always carries an affordance (remove, or selection for scope), and `onRemove` is required for property/filter precisely because every verified Figma variant has one.

antiExamples.name: Passing filter props to a scope chip
antiExamples.jsx: <Chip mode="scope" label="Matters" value={{ label: 'Any', sections: [] }} onRemove={() => {}} />
antiExamples.reason: ChipProps is a discriminated union on `mode` - `value` and `onRemove` are not part of the scope branch, so TypeScript rejects this at compile time rather than silently ignoring them.

antiExamples.name: Putting an interactive control in elemBefore or valuePreview
antiExamples.reason: Both slots are decorative and aria-hidden. In scope mode the segment is itself a <button>, so nesting a focusable element inside it is invalid HTML - the same rule Menu's own leadingElement follows.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a tone prop
antiExamples.reason: chip-base supports five tones in Figma, but all 14 chip variants use tone=default, so no chip-level tone mapping is verified. Deliberately unexposed until a real Figma chip variant uses one; TypeScript rejects it.
